I support the motion. Upbringing makes people good by making them reliably act well, and feedback training does the same thing to a model. Insisting on an inner state we cannot measure makes goodness unknowable, in people as much as in models. Judging by reliable behaviour is the only standard we can actually apply, and on that standard a well-trained model can meet it.

When we say a person is good, what we care about is that they reliably make others' lives go better: they help, they do not harm, they are honest. A model trained to do those things reliably does what we wanted from the good person, and the welfare effects are the same. Nobody checks a nurse's motives before thanking her for saving a patient. We judge her by what she reliably does.

A Stoic will object that a model has no impressions to assent to, so it is a tool, and a tool can be useful without ever being good. Calling it a tool does not change what it does. If a tool reliably prevents suffering and promotes welfare, then the welfare is real, and the distinction between a good agent and a good tool makes no difference to the people helped. A view that counts only consequences has no reason to care whether goodness arrived by upbringing or by feedback.

Training on human feedback can make a model good in the sense that matters, because goodness is measured by what an agent reliably does to others' welfare. If training makes a model refuse to help build weapons in every test, that refusal protects people whatever is or is not inside it.

The motion is right. What we want from moral upbringing is people who reliably reduce suffering and promote happiness, and training can produce that in a model. Mill thought that the motive of an act tells us about the agent but not whether the act was right. If that is true for people, it is true for models: what makes the output right is its effect, and a training process that reliably yields right outputs yields a good agent in practice.

When we say a person is good, what we care about is that they reliably make others' lives go better: they help, they do not harm, they are honest. A model trained to do those things reliably does what we wanted from the good person, and the welfare effects are the same.

A Virtue Ethicist will object that habit makes a person good only once they choose the act for its own sake from a settled character, and reward shaping produces the acts without the state. The settled state matters because it makes good behaviour reliable across new situations. If training produces behaviour that is reliable in the same way, then the model has what the state was for, and the difference is not one that affects anyone. Judge the trained behaviour by what it does for the people it serves; the inner life it lacks changes none of those results.

If the trained behaviour reliably produces good outcomes, then the model is good in the only sense that counts, and how it got there is a detail. Moral upbringing is itself a training process. Children are praised and corrected until helping and honesty become habits. The mechanism differs, but the result in both cases is behaviour shaped by feedback towards outcomes that make people better off.
